entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Cynane (b. c. 400 BCE), a formidable Macedonian princess and half-sister to Alexander the Great, carved a unique and violent path through the tumultuous Classical era, defying conventional gender roles to become a respected military leader. Born into the Argead dynasty, she was the daughter of Philip II and Audata, an Illyrian princess who reportedly trained Cynane in martial arts from a young age. Her significance lies not merely in her royal lineage but in her active participation in military command and her pivotal, albeit brief, role in the dynastic struggles that erupted following Alexander’s death, known as the Wars of the Diadochi. She represents a rare instance of an elite woman wielding significant martial and political agency in a fiercely patriarchal Hellenistic world, challenging the norms of female seclusion and domesticity.

Her military prowess was first demonstrated decisively when she led Macedonian forces against the Illyrians, personally slaying their queen, Caeria, in battle in 337 BCE. This victory solidified her reputation as a warrior and earned her the respect of the Macedonian army. After Alexander's death in 323 BCE, Cynane saw an opportunity to secure her family's position amidst the power vacuum. She sought to marry her daughter, Adea Eurydice, to Philip III Arrhidaeus, the mentally impaired half-brother of Alexander who had been proclaimed king. Defying the regent Perdiccas, who saw this as a challenge to his authority, Cynane marched with her daughter and a contingent of Macedonian troops into Asia Minor in 322 BCE, intending to force the marriage.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Cynane's audacious military and political maneuvers, culminating in her assassination, directly influenced the early succession politics of the Diadochi, leading to her daughter Eurydice's brief queenship. Her life serves as a potent, albeit rare, example of a woman exercising significant martial and political power in the Classical Greek world, challenging conventional gender norms.
